newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: KL INTERBANK RATES UP SLIGHTLY ON LACK OF OFFERS.
newsitem.headline: KL INTERBANK RATES UP SLIGHTLY ON LACK OF OFFERS.

text.p: Malaysian interbank rates rose slightly on Wednesday morning after an agent bank of Bank Negara Malaysia stopped lending, dealers said.
"An agent bank was lending one-month money at 7.25 percent this morning but when it stopped offering, rates went back up," said a dealer at a Malaysian bank.
At 0330 GMT, the one-month was at 7.3/4 percent against 7.25 percent on Tuesday.
One-week money was steady at 6.2/4 percent and three-month was also unchanged at 7.5 percent.
Dealers said the market was getting tight again as funds which banks borrowed from the central bank in July were starting to mature and leave the system.

Bank Negara has been lending funds, mostly one-month money, over the past month to help ease market tightness and bring interbank rates down, dealers said. Massive intervention by the central bank in the foreign exchange market in June to defend the ringgit from speculative attack had earlier caused a liquidity squeeze in the money market.
"We will see whether Negara injects the funds back into the market," said another dealer.
Interest rate futures on the Malaysia Monetary Exchange extended their rise on expectations of softening of interbank rates, futures market dealers said.
At 0330 GMT, the three-month Kuala Lumpur Interbank Offered Rate (KLIBOR) September contract was up three points to 92.50, or an implied yield of 7.50 percent.
The December contract rose two to 92.67, or 7.33 percent while March 1998 was also up two to 92.74, or 7.26 percent.
